chapter_theme: Understanding shown in conduct: restraint toward fallen foes and in poverty, judging people by mind and conduct rather than birthplace or kind, steadiness in friendship, and knowing that a person raises or lowers himself. It ends with the picture of a life that completes work, pleasure and virtue.
structure_note: The quatrains range from conduct toward enemies and superiors (241, 249) and in poverty (242), through birth and environment (243 to 245) and friendship (244, 246, 247), to the self as the cause of one's standing (248) and a whole life well finished (250).

241.reading: When the worthy see their enemies humbled, they themselves feel shame and do not advance on them; see, the snake whose strength nothing can trouble does not seize the moon while it is a young crescent.
241.nuance: The shame belongs to the victor, not the defeated. Shanmuganar names the snake as Rahu, the eclipse serpent.

242.reading: Lord of the cool shore of the vast sea, for the poor, restraint is the ornament; if one lives without humility and beyond measure, the town one lives in will speak ill of one's family.
242.nuance: The cost of a poor man's lack of restraint falls on his lineage, not only on himself.

243.reading: In whatever soil it is sown, a strychnos seed will not become a coconut; since even those of the south enter heaven, one's next world comes from oneself, and in the north too there are very many idle wasters.
243.nuance: Pope calls the northerners 'denizens of hell'; கொன்னாளர் means those who spend their days to no purpose, which is milder.

positions.position: The south is the Tamil land, and the verse rebuts a northern claim that those born there cannot reach a good state.
The south is Yama's quarter, the direction of death, rather than a region of people.

244.reading: Though ripened among neem leaves, the plantain keeps its sweet taste unchanged; so, though their company is bad, the friendship of those of good nature rarely turns to a bad mind.
244.nuance: Pope reads இனம் as 'race'; both commentators read it as the company one keeps.

245.reading: Lord of the cool shore of the dashing sea, since sweet water rises even beside the sea and brackish water even on the hills, people are not as their kind but as their minds.

positions.position: People are simply not like those of their own group; the mind decides.
People are judged not only by their group but by their minds as well, so group still counts.

246.reading: Lord of the cool shore where thick-trunked punnai trees grow, do people of steady mind, who stay with whomever they have formed a good bond, leave and then rejoin? It is good not to mix with people indiscriminately.
246.nuance: Pope takes விராய் as alternating warmth and coldness; both commentators take it as mixing with people without examination.

247.reading: Join those whose understanding grasps things as they should be grasped, and joy joins you; if you join those without discernment, the pain parts only when you part from them.
247.nuance: The verse is built on repeated words (உணர உணரும், புணரப் புணரும், தெரியத் தெரியும், பிரியப் பிரியும்), a figure Mudaliar names.

248.reading: The one who sets a person in a good state, the one who unsettles and casts him down, the one who raises him ever higher, and the one who makes him the head of others, is that person himself.
248.nuance: Mudaliar names the cause as one's understanding or lack of it; the verse itself names none. It also names no fate, which sits uneasily with chapter 11 on old deeds, unless those deeds are counted as one's own doing too.

249.reading: Lord of the cool shore of the roaring sea, when even the great follow behind the unlearned for the sake of a task, that is not folly but understanding.
249.nuance: The verse allows status to be set aside for a purpose (கரும வரிசையால்); it doesn't say the great should follow the unlearned in general.

250.reading: If one does one's work, enjoys one's pleasures, and does virtuous giving to the worthy, and all three are completed without hindrance in a single life, people call it a ship that has reached the port.
250.nuance: A full worldly life is praised here, in a work that mostly urges renunciation, through the image of a trading voyage brought home. Pope reads ஒருநிலையே as 'in this one state'; Shanmuganar as 'all together'.

links.note: 773 calls fierceness valour and kindness to a foe who has fallen (ஊராண்மை) its keen edge. 241 says the worthy feel shame to attack a humbled foe.

879 says to cut a thorn tree while it is young, before it can wound the cutter; 241 says the worthy don't attack an enemy at his weakest. Both concern whether to strike a foe while he is weak. The tension holds if 879's thorn tree is an enemy, as Parimelazhagar reads it in the chapter on enmity.

Both use the eclipse snake and the moon. In 148 the moon still lights the world while the snake holds half of it, an image of the nobly born in poverty; in 241 the snake spares the crescent, an image of the worthy sparing a humbled foe.

963 says humility suits prosperity and standing tall suits adversity; 242 says restraint is the ornament of the poor and that living without humility shames one's family. Both concern how the poor should bear themselves. The tension depends on taking 963's உயர்வு as not bowing, as Parimelazhagar glosses it, and 242's அடக்கம் as bowing; if 242 condemns only living beyond one's means, they fit.
125 says humility is good for all and an extra wealth for the rich. 242 makes it the ornament of the poor.
Both deny that origin decides worth: 972 says all are alike in birth and differ by their deeds, and 243 says the next world comes from oneself, not from one's region.
195 calls good and bad caste mere words and puts worth in austerity, learning and effort; 243 makes the same claim about the region of one's birth.

179 says goodness perishes when it comes near bad company, as a storm wrecks a ship; 244 says the good-natured do not turn bad in mind though their company is bad. Both concern whether bad company corrupts the good, and the commentators read 244's இனம் as company, which makes the conflict direct.
458 says that even those with full goodness of mind are strengthened by good company. 244 says the good-natured hold firm without it, even among bad company.

The same image of water leads to opposite claims. 452 says water changes with the soil, so a person's understanding takes on the nature of their company (454 adds that it only seems to be in the mind); 245 says sweet water rises by the sea, so people are as their minds, not their kind. The tension holds if 245's இனம் means the people around one, as the image of surroundings suggests. Shanmuganar's 'not only by their group' softens it.
Both condemn friendship that comes and goes. 215 contrasts the tree flower with the pond flower; 246 says people of steady mind don't leave and rejoin.

168 says parting even from those without discernment brings great pain, so it is best to mix with none; 247 says that parting from the undiscerning is how the pain parts. Both concern whether leaving the undiscerning hurts, and they share the phrase தெரியத் தெரியும் தெரிவிலா. The tension rests on reading 247 as both commentators and Pope do.
Both tie joy to good company and affliction to bad: no greater support than good company and nothing more afflicting than bad (460).
192 says a pliant twig becomes a post for tethering elephants, and so does a life if a man makes himself without slackening; 248 says a person alone raises or lowers himself.
505 makes one's own deeds the touchstone of greatness and smallness; 248 makes the self the agent of rising and falling.
Both permit the capable to stoop for a purpose: the tiger eats a frog when there is no other meat (193), and the great walk behind the unlearned for a task (249).

967 says it is better to be ruined than to live by following those who scorn you. 249 allows following the unlearned for the sake of a task, which marks a limit on that pride: following for a purpose is not following for a living.
114 names the three ends of life and says gaining the middle one, wealth, brings the other two. 250 pictures a life that completes all three without hindrance, as a ship reaching port.
754 says rightly gained wealth yields virtue and pleasure. 250 counts the life that achieves work, pleasure and virtuous giving together as a voyage completed.

source_issues: 246: the Tamil has 'ம்ருஉச்செய்' where Mudaliar's gloss has மரூஉ.
247: the Tamil has a corrupted character (புணா஢ன் for புணரின்).
249 and 250: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned.
250: Pope's text ends with a separator line, and the shanmuganar field ends with the header of chapter 26.
